name: Yoga / Surya Namaskar for height

lead: Some height programmes and forum threads promote yoga stretches and Surya Namaskar (Sun Salutation), a flowing sequence of about twelve linked postures, as a way to stand taller. The payoff people want is a lengthened, decompressed spine and better posture.

Proponents say the stretching lengthens the spine and improves posture, a route to a small change in standing height. Published studies of Sun Salutation measure energy use (about 2.9 to 7.4 METs) and muscle activation, and none was found measuring height.

paras: People do the sequence or a stretching routine regularly, often in the morning, and combine it with other posture and height habits. Results people look for are better posture and a more upright stance over weeks of practice.
Yoga is generally an ordinary physical activity with the usual strain risks. No height-specific harms are documented.

angle.text: Yoga and Surya Namaskar are used as stretching routines to lengthen the spine and improve posture so you stand a little taller. Research on yoga covers fitness and flexibility rather than height.

lead: Yoga and Surya Namaskar (Sun Salutation) appear in height-increase programmes and forum threads as a daily stretching routine for looking taller. Surya Namaskar is a flowing sequence of about twelve linked postures associated with Hindu devotion to the sun god Surya.[1] People who use it for height generally aim at posture and spinal length: standing straighter, extending the spine and reducing slouch can add visible centimetres to standing height without changing bone length.

The Sun Salutation's history is uncertain. No hatha yoga text recorded the sequence before the 19th century, and it was popularised in the early 20th century, including through a 1928 publication by the Rajah of Aundh and the teaching of Krishnamacharya.[1] Hatha yoga more broadly was reshaped in the 20th century into a posture-based fitness practice that spread worldwide.[2]

Published research on Surya Namaskar concerns energy expenditure and muscle activation, such as an energy cost ranging from roughly 2.9 to 7.4 METs depending on style, rather than height outcomes.[1] Reference works describe adult height as determined mainly by genetics and childhood conditions.[3]

paras: Height-focused programmes typically present stretching poses, spinal extensions and the Sun Salutation sequence as ways to lengthen the spine and improve alignment. Variations differ by yoga school, including Iyengar, Sivananda and Ashtanga.[1]

In the looksmaxxing forum discussion, the idea is usually that daily yoga stretches the spine and corrects posture, for a possible half inch to an inch of standing height, and that it could help limit height loss with age. Proponents in these threads explicitly say it does not make bones grow; they describe it as making a person look taller through posture.[4] Some posters pair it with chin tucks.[4]

Wikipedia's article on human height reports that height varies through the day, with a study of 100 children finding an average drop of about 1.5 cm from waking to late afternoon, and that age-related shrinkage is attributed to drying of spinal discs, soft-tissue loss and posture changes.[3] Genetics accounts for an estimated 60 to 80 percent of height differences, and growth typically ends around age 18 to 19 in males.[3]
Posture-oriented routines such as yoga work on the soft-tissue and postural side of this picture. Studies of yoga for height as an outcome have not been found.

A 2014 study measured muscle activity during Ashtanga sequences and found different muscle use in beginners and instructors, and a 2016 systematic review placed the energy cost of Sun Salutation from light to vigorous depending on style.[1] These studies did not measure height.

Broader yoga research in the literature covers depression, anxiety, stress measures and low back pain, for example systematic reviews and randomized trials of yoga for low back pain and for anxiety.[5][6]

No studies found measuring height change from yoga or Surya Namaskar. Related randomized trials of yoga cover other outcomes, such as virtual yoga for chronic low back pain and meta-analyses for anxiety.[5][6]

lore.intro: Yoga for height appears mainly in marketing and in height-gain forum threads as a gentle, low-cost routine aimed at posture and spinal length.[4]
